en: The amihan brings cool, dry air to the Philippines between November and February.
Volcanic ash from Mount Mayon weathers into highly fertile soil ideal for growing abaca plants.
The Puerto Princesa Subterranean River flows through massive limestone caves carved by groundwater in Palawan.
Towering cumulonimbus clouds produce heavy afternoon rain showers and thunderstorms commonly observed in the Philippines.
During a solar eclipse, the moon passes directly between the Earth and the sun, blocking sunlight.
Filipino farmers historically used the visible Orion constellation, locally called Balatik, to signal the planting season.
A full moon appears completely illuminated because the Earth is positioned directly between the sun and moon.
Storm surges during typhoons cause abnormal rises in sea level that flood coastal areas in the Philippines.
Dark, fine-grained basalt rocks form when hot lava from Philippine volcanoes cools rapidly on the surface.
Cool mountain air in Baguio City causes water vapor to condense into thick, observable fog.
Tropical plants like banana trees release water vapor into the air through tiny leaf pores during transpiration.
A sea breeze occurs when cooler air from the ocean moves inland to replace rising warm air.
